r.정치 구도: Cuba is a one-party state in which only the Communist Party is legal. The Castro brothers, who led the 1959 revolution, ran the country for more than 60 years, and when the younger brother stepped down as party first secretary in 2021, the revolutionary generation left frontline politics. The 2019 constitution separated the posts of president and prime minister and limited the president to two five-year terms. In July 2021, protests over power cuts and food shortages broke out across the island, and many people were arrested. The government legalized small and medium private businesses in 2021, and in June 2026 it passed reforms letting private firms employ more than 100 people and import and export directly. Officials say they studied the Chinese and Vietnamese models, while insisting the country is not turning to capitalism.

t.why: Lying about 150 km across the sea from Florida, Cuba has been a US security concern since the Cold War. In 1962 the Soviet Union's attempt to install nuclear missiles there brought the two superpowers to the brink of war, and the United States has kept an economic embargo in place since that era. Relations were restored in 2015, but the embargo is written into US law and remains, while the UN General Assembly votes by a wide margin every year to call for its end. After the United States seized Venezuela's president in January 2026, the Venezuelan oil Cuba relied on stopped arriving. When Washington threatened tariffs on any country supplying Cuba with oil, Mexico halted its shipments too, and since then nationwide blackouts have recurred, food and medicine have run short, and even the free health care system is faltering. Cuba has also built influence in Latin America and Africa through medical diplomacy, sending doctors abroad in exchange for hard currency.
t.rel: It broke off relations with the United States across the sea in 1961 and restored them in 2015, but the embargo remains. The US base at Guantanamo sits on the island's southeast. It has traded doctors for Venezuelan oil and is close to Russia and China.
t.korea: South Korea and Cuba established diplomatic relations in February 2024, making Cuba the 193rd country to have ties with Seoul. Cuba had been close to North Korea since 1960, which is why it had no relations with South Korea for so long. A South Korean embassy opened in Havana in January 2025. In 1921, Koreans who had worked on henequen plantations in Mexico moved to Cuba and settled there, and about 1,100 of their descendants still live across the island. Despite grueling farm work, those early migrants raised money for Korea's independence movement.
t.know: Cuba and the United States broke off relations after the 1959 revolution and only reopened embassies in 2015.
etext: Caribbean beaches and old Havana have drawn tourists and brought in foreign currency. But visitors have not returned to pre-COVID levels, and blackouts and shortages have slowed the recovery.
Sending doctors and nurses abroad, paid for by host governments, is a major source of hard currency. Cuba has also built a biotech industry that makes its own vaccines and medicines.
It mines and sells nickel and cobalt, and Cuban cigars are a world-famous export. The sugar industry has shrunk sharply as its equipment aged.

The US embargo makes it hard to borrow money or buy goods. Old power plants and the loss of imported oil mean frequent blackouts, and a wide gap between the official and market exchange rates has fueled inflation. A large exodus of young people adds to the strain.
